question: What is the landing gear arrangement?

options.text: Tandem main gear with outrigger wheels
Tricycle, with four wheels on each main gear
Tricycle, with two wheels on each main gear and two on the nose gear
Tricycle, with a single wheel on each main gear

explanation: Two wheels per leg gives redundancy against a tyre failure while keeping the weight and the wheel well size down.

question: In which direction does the main landing gear retract?

options.text: Inboard into the wheel well
Forward into the wing root
Outboard into the wing
Rearward into the engine nacelle

explanation: Retracting towards the fuselage keeps the wheel well inside the centre section where the structure is deepest.

question: What is unusual about the main wheel well on this type?

options.text: The wheels retract into a fairing outside the fuselage
The wheel well is pressurised in flight
The wheels are enclosed by doors that remain open in flight
The wheels are not enclosed by doors and seal against the well

explanation: Omitting the doors saves weight and complexity, with the tyre itself forming the aerodynamic seal.

question: In which direction does the nose gear retract?

options.text: Sideways to the left
Forward
Vertically upward
Rearward

explanation: Retracting forward means that if the gear is unlocked it tends to fall and lock under its own weight and the airflow.

question: Why is forward retraction of the nose gear an advantage during a manual extension?

options.text: It prevents the gear from being retracted again by mistake
It allows the gear doors to close afterwards
It reduces the hydraulic volume required
The airflow and gravity both assist the gear towards the down and locked position

explanation: A free falling gear that is helped by the airstream is more reliable than one that has to be pushed against it.

question: What are the positions of the landing gear lever?

options.text: RETRACT, HOLD and EXTEND
UP, NEUTRAL and DOWN
UP and DOWN only
UP, OFF and DOWN

explanation: The intermediate position exists to remove hydraulic pressure from the system once the gear is up.

question: Why is the gear lever placed in the OFF position after retraction?

options.text: To depressurise the gear system and avoid continuous pressure on the components
To arm the manual extension system
To allow the gear doors to close
To transfer the gear system to the standby hydraulics

explanation: Leaving the system pressurised throughout the flight would heat the fluid and stress the seals unnecessarily.

question: What does a green landing gear indication light show?

options.text: That gear is up and locked
That the gear doors are closed
That gear is in transit
That gear is down and locked

explanation: Three green lights are the confirmation that the airplane is actually configured for landing.

question: What does a red landing gear indication light show?

options.text: The gear brakes are overheating
The gear is in transit or disagrees with the lever position
The gear has been manually extended
The gear is down and locked

explanation: It highlights a disagreement between what has been selected and what has actually happened.

question: How is the landing gear extended if the normal hydraulic system is unavailable?

options.text: Manual extension handles release the uplocks and the gear free falls
The standby hydraulic system extends the gear
A pneumatic bottle blows the gear down
An electric motor drives the gear down

explanation: Gravity and the airflow do the work, so no second power source is required for extension.

question: What is the operational consequence of a manual gear extension?

options.text: The gear must be extended below a reduced speed limit only
The nose wheel steering becomes unavailable
The gear cannot be retracted again until maintenance action
The brakes revert to the accumulator supply

explanation: The decision commits the airplane to flying with the gear down, with the associated drag and speed limits.

question: Where are the manual gear extension access points located?

options.text: In the main wheel well
In the forward cargo compartment
Under the first observer seat
On the flight deck floor behind the control pedestal

explanation: They are reachable in flight without leaving the flight deck, which is what makes the procedure practical.

question: How is nose wheel steering controlled at low speed for large angles?

options.text: By the rudder pedals
By the steering tiller
By the autopilot rollout mode
By differential braking only

explanation: The tiller provides the large deflections needed for turns on the ground, well beyond what the pedals can command.

question: What steering authority is available through the rudder pedals?

options.text: Full authority above 60 kt only
A limited nose wheel deflection for directional control during the takeoff and landing roll
No nose wheel authority at all
The same authority as the tiller

explanation: Small pedal authority keeps directional control available without the risk of a large inadvertent input at speed.

question: Why is the tiller not used at high ground speed?

options.text: Because the tiller is disconnected above a set speed
Because the hydraulic supply is inhibited above taxi speed
Because a large steering input at speed can cause a loss of directional control or gear damage
Because the nose wheel is unloaded above that speed

explanation: The technique and the speeds involved are procedural. Verify the guidance against your operator manuals.

question: What type of brakes are fitted to the main wheels?

options.text: Single disc brakes
Expander tube brakes
Drum brakes
Multiple disc brakes

explanation: Multiple discs provide the very large energy absorption a rejected takeoff demands within a compact wheel.

question: What does the brake wear indicator show?

options.text: The number of landings since the brake was fitted
The remaining wear available in the brake pack
The hydraulic pressure applied to the brake
The brake temperature after landing

explanation: It is checked with the brakes applied, since the measurement depends on the discs being compressed.

question: What is the purpose of the antiskid system?

options.text: It prevents the wheels from locking and preserves braking effectiveness
It distributes braking evenly between the two main gears
It applies the brakes automatically after touchdown
It limits the maximum brake temperature

explanation: A locked wheel produces less retardation than a rolling wheel at the point of maximum friction, and it destroys the tyre.

question: What is touchdown protection in the antiskid system?

options.text: It prevents brake application until the wheels have spun up
It limits the brake pressure during the first seconds after landing
It inhibits the autobrakes until the nose wheel is down
It releases the brakes if the airplane bounces

explanation: Braking a wheel that is not yet turning would guarantee a skid at the moment of touchdown.

question: What is locked wheel protection?

options.text: It locks the wheels when the parking brake is applied
It prevents brake application with the gear retracted
It releases the brake on a wheel that has stopped while others are still rotating
It prevents the parking brake from being set in flight

explanation: Comparing the wheels with each other is what allows the system to detect a skid that is already established.

question: What is the effect of an inoperative antiskid system on landing performance?

options.text: The brakes become unavailable below 60 kt
Only the autobrake settings are affected
There is no effect provided the runway is dry
The landing distance required increases significantly

explanation: Without skid protection the achievable braking is limited by what the pilot dares apply without locking a wheel.

question: What are the autobrake selections available?

options.text: On and off only
A single setting armed automatically
Low, medium and high only
A rejected takeoff setting and several landing settings

explanation: The rejected takeoff setting is a ground only selection, while the numbered settings target a deceleration rate on landing.

question: How do the numbered autobrake settings work?

options.text: They modulate the brakes to a selected stopping distance
They apply the brake pressure required to achieve a target deceleration rate
They apply a fixed brake pressure for each setting
They apply the brakes for a fixed time after touchdown

explanation: Because a rate is targeted, the use of reverse thrust reduces the braking the system applies rather than adding to it.

question: What is the consequence of using heavy reverse thrust with a low autobrake setting?

options.text: The antiskid system is inhibited
The autobrakes reduce brake pressure to hold the target deceleration
The deceleration increases beyond the selected rate
The autobrakes disarm automatically

explanation: The system is targeting a rate, so anything else that decelerates the airplane is compensated for by less braking.

question: When does the rejected takeoff autobrake setting apply the brakes?

options.text: Only when the speedbrakes deploy
At V1 regardless of thrust lever position
When the thrust levers are retarded to idle above a threshold speed on the ground
Immediately when the setting is selected

explanation: Retarding the thrust levers is the pilot decision to stop, and the system acts on it immediately.

question: What level of braking does the rejected takeoff setting apply?

options.text: Maximum braking
A fixed moderate pressure
The same as the highest numbered landing setting
A deceleration rate matched to the runway remaining

explanation: A rejected takeoff near V1 uses all the remaining runway, so there is no reason to hold anything back.

question: What causes the autobrakes to disarm?

options.text: Manual braking, advancing the thrust levers or moving the speedbrake lever down
Reverse thrust selection
Reaching taxi speed
Nose wheel touchdown

explanation: Each of these is an unambiguous indication that the pilot has taken over or no longer wants automatic braking.

question: What does the autobrake disarm light indicate?

options.text: The antiskid system is inoperative
The parking brake is set
The brakes are overheating
The autobrake system is no longer armed or has failed

explanation: It tells the crew that the expected automatic braking will not happen, which matters before touchdown and after it.

question: Why is a higher autobrake setting not always the better choice?

options.text: Because high settings disable reverse thrust
Because high settings are unavailable on wet runways
Because high settings cannot be disarmed manually
Because a high deceleration is uncomfortable and raises brake temperatures unnecessarily

explanation: The setting is chosen for the runway available and the conditions, not as a default maximum.

question: How is the parking brake held on?

options.text: By a mechanical latch on the brake pedals
By pressure stored in the brake accumulator
By continuous hydraulic system pressure
By an electric actuator on each brake unit

explanation: Stored pressure is what allows the brake to be left set with no hydraulic system running.

question: Why should the parking brake not be set on very hot brakes?

options.text: Because the antiskid system is inhibited when parked
Because holding the brakes applied prevents cooling and can cause damage or a fire
Because the brake wear indicators become unreliable
Because the accumulator cannot hold pressure at high temperature

explanation: Airflow around a released brake is the main cooling path, and clamping the discs together traps the heat.

question: What determines brake energy absorbed during a stop?

options.text: The runway surface condition alone
The number of brake applications made
The airplane weight and the speed from which it is stopped
The autobrake setting alone

explanation: Energy rises with the square of the speed, which is why a high speed rejected takeoff is so severe on the brakes.

question: Why is a cooling period sometimes required before the next departure?

options.text: Because hot brakes cannot hold the parking brake
Because the antiskid system requires a temperature reset
Because hot brakes may not absorb the energy of a rejected takeoff
Because the tyres cannot be inflated while hot

explanation: The brakes must start the takeoff with enough capacity remaining to stop the airplane if the takeoff is rejected.

question: What is the purpose of the fusible plugs in the wheels?

options.text: They prevent the tyre from being over inflated
They indicate that the brake has been overheated
They release tyre pressure in a controlled way if the wheel becomes too hot
They seal the wheel against hydraulic fluid leakage

explanation: A controlled deflation is far safer than a tyre bursting under heat, particularly with people working around the airplane.

question: Why are personnel kept clear of the wheels after a high energy stop?

options.text: Because the gear may retract unexpectedly
Because hydraulic fluid may be sprayed from the brake lines
Because of the risk of a tyre or wheel failure while the brakes are hot
Because the brakes continue to apply automatically

explanation: The danger zone is to the sides of the wheels, and it persists for a considerable time after the airplane has stopped.

question: What does a brake temperature indication allow the crew to do?

options.text: Establish the brake wear remaining
Judge whether the brakes have enough remaining capacity for the next departure
Determine when the parking brake can be released
Set the correct autobrake level for landing

explanation: It converts a judgement about the previous landing into a decision about the next takeoff.

question: What is the purpose of the air ground sensing system?

options.text: It senses the extension of the landing gear
It measures the weight on each landing gear leg
It tells airplane systems whether the airplane is on the ground or airborne
It detects the compression of the shock struts for maintenance

explanation: Many systems change their behaviour completely between the two states, and they all depend on this single input.

question: Which of the following depends on the air ground logic?

options.text: The hydraulic reservoir pressurisation
The stabiliser trim range
The fuel crossfeed valve position
Automatic speedbrake deployment and the ground spoiler function

explanation: Deploying lift destroying devices in flight would be catastrophic, so they are interlocked with the ground signal.

question: What is the consequence of an erroneous air ground signal?

options.text: Systems may behave as though the airplane is in the wrong state, affecting warnings and configurations
Only the landing gear indication is affected
The gear cannot be retracted
The autobrakes become unavailable but nothing else changes

explanation: A single wrong input propagates into many systems, which is why the failure can be confusing in the air.

question: When does the landing gear warning horn sound?

options.text: When the parking brake is set with the engines running
Whenever the gear is in transit
When the airplane is configured for landing without the gear down and locked
When the gear is extended above the limit speed

explanation: It is a configuration warning tied to flap position, thrust and height, which is where a gear up landing becomes possible.

question: Why is part of the landing gear warning unable to be silenced?

options.text: Because the silencing switch is only accessible from the observer seat
Because in the landing configuration a gear up landing is imminent and the warning must not be suppressed
Because the horn shares a circuit with the fire bell
Because the warning is generated by the flight management computer

explanation: A warning that can be cancelled will eventually be cancelled, which is unacceptable at the point of landing.

question: What is the difference between the gear operating and gear extended speed limits?

options.text: One applies to moving the gear and the other to flying with it extended
One applies to manual extension and the other to normal extension
One applies in the climb and the other in the descent
One applies with flaps up and the other with flaps extended

explanation: The doors and the actuating mechanism are the limiting structure while the gear is moving. Verify the speeds against your operator FCOM.

question: Why is the gear operating speed limit lower than the gear extended limit?

options.text: Because the hydraulic pressure is insufficient at higher speeds
Because the gear cannot lock at higher speeds
Because the doors and the mechanism are exposed to the airflow during the transit
Because the tyres would be damaged by the airflow

explanation: Once the gear is down and locked the structure is in its strongest configuration, which allows a higher speed.

question: What is the function of the shock strut?

options.text: It transmits the antiskid signal to the wheel
It absorbs the vertical energy of the landing and the loads during taxi
It steers the nose wheel
It provides the mounting for the brake unit

explanation: It is an oleo pneumatic unit, using fluid and gas to absorb and damp the loads rather than simply spring them back.

question: Why is correct shock strut inflation important?

options.text: Because it sets the nose wheel steering authority
Because an incorrectly inflated strut changes the landing loads and the air ground sensing
Because it determines the brake pressure available
Because it affects the tyre pressure indication

explanation: The strut extension is what the ground sensing proximity switches measure, so its condition affects more than ride quality.

question: Why is tyre pressure significant to operations?

options.text: It changes the gear retraction time
It determines the maximum braking available
It affects the autobrake deceleration target
An underinflated tyre overheats and can fail, and it changes the load sharing between the pair

explanation: When one tyre of a pair is soft the other carries more than its share, which is how a single failure becomes two.

question: What is the significance of a failed tyre on the same gear leg during the takeoff roll?

options.text: There is no effect until the gear is retracted
The remaining tyre carries the full load and may also fail
The gear will not retract
The antiskid system will lock the corresponding brake

explanation: Tyre failures on a pair are a recognised sequence, which is why debris on the runway after a tyre failure is treated seriously.

question: Why is a landing gear vibration or noise after takeoff investigated before retraction?

options.text: Because a damaged gear or tyre may jam in the wheel well or fail to extend later
Because the gear warning system cannot detect damage
Because vibration indicates a hydraulic leak
Because the gear must be retracted within a time limit

explanation: The wheel well is a confined space, and damaged components brought into it can become unrecoverable problems.

question: What provides braking if both the normal and alternate brake systems are lost?

options.text: The brake accumulator, for a limited number of applications
The standby hydraulic system
The autobrake system on its own reservoir
The parking brake only, applied fully

explanation: The accumulator holds a finite quantity of pressurised fluid, so every application consumes part of what remains.

question: Why is antiskid protection a consideration when braking on accumulator pressure?

options.text: Because the accumulator provides too little pressure to lock a wheel
Because the antiskid system consumes accumulator pressure
Because the accumulator is isolated from the antiskid valves
Because the protection may not be available, so the braking technique must avoid locking a wheel

explanation: Steady and progressive application replaces the electronic protection when that protection is not there.

question: Why is differential braking an unsatisfactory substitute for nose wheel steering?

options.text: It disables the antiskid system
It is prohibited on all runway surfaces
It cannot be used with the parking brake charged
It is coarse, it heats the brakes and it provides little control at low speed

explanation: It works well enough to clear a runway, but it is not a technique for manoeuvring an airplane around a ramp.

question: What is the purpose of the gear position indication being independent of the lever position?

options.text: So the crew can see what the gear has actually done rather than what was selected
So the gear can be monitored during manual extension only
So the indication remains available after a hydraulic failure
So the indication can be tested on the ground

explanation: The whole value of the indication rests on it reporting the real state of the uplocks and downlocks.

question: Why does a green indication for one gear and a red for another require particular care?

options.text: Because the gear lever must be recycled immediately
Because the gear warning horn will not sound
Because a partially extended gear may collapse on landing
Because the autobrakes will not arm

explanation: A leg that is not locked can fold under load, which changes both the landing technique and the choice of runway.

question: What happens to the wheels when the gear is retracted?

options.text: They are braked automatically to stop rotation
They are locked by the parking brake system
They continue to rotate freely in the wheel well
They are slowed by contact with the well seals only

explanation: A spinning wheel brought into the well would create vibration and could damage the structure and the tyre.

question: Why is the landing gear system described as having independent extension and retraction paths?

options.text: Because extension uses system B and retraction uses system A
Because both use the standby system in an emergency
Because extension can be achieved without hydraulic power while retraction cannot
Because retraction can be achieved manually but extension cannot

explanation: Only extension is essential for a safe landing, so only extension is given an alternative means.
